title: Fallback-first ops playbook: self-hosted inference comparison and GTM messaging
content:
TL;DR:
This brief creates a compact, sales- and ops-focused playbook for positioning Redwood against modern self-hosted stacks (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM and similar) with a ‘fallback-first’ framing: highlight where customers should own inference, where they should rent it, and how Redwood reduces operational risk by making graceful degradation and cost controls a first-class feature.

Audience:
- GTM: account execs, solutions engineers, pre-sales
- Product: pricing and packaging owners
- Technical sales enablement and docs

Objective:
- Give crisp messaging hooks for conversations with infra/platform teams and ML engineers evaluating self-hosted options
- Provide a short technical comparator that surfaces real operational failure modes (not just latency numbers)
- Offer a recommended pilot/migration path and a starter objection-response playbook

1) One-line positioning for sales
- "Run inference where you want; keep your app resilient where you must."
- Supporting point: Redwood lets you keep control over latency/cost targets while avoiding the maintenance tax of custom inference stacks.

2) Buyer personas and primary concerns
- Platform/Infra Lead (SRE/Platform): reliability, predictable capacity, backups for spot instance failures, autoscaling, security (VPC/KMS).
- ML Engineer: flexible model formats, quantization support, local debugging, performance parity with bare-metal GPUs.
- Product Engineering Manager: feature SLAs, latency percentiles, cost per active user, rollout safety.

3) Tech comparator (short, operational lens)
- vLLM-style stacks (open-source, batch-oriented):
  - Strengths: cheap at steady-state for long-context workloads, flexible research iteration, runs on commodity infra.
  - Weaknesses: operator burden (KV cache correctness, memory fragmentation), brittle tail-latency under bursty traffic, manual kernel tuning for multiple model sizes.
  - Failure modes we hear: sudden OOM on large sequence lengths, high GC-like pauses after many small requests, cache invalidation bugs during model swaps.

- Text Generation Inference (TGI)/Ray-based ecosystems:
  - Strengths: integrated serving + APIs, good dev ergonomics for conversation patterns, often simpler batching layer.
  - Weaknesses: scaling across heterogeneous GPUs is ad hoc, inconsistent autoscaler defaults, limited fallback policies across regions.
  - Failure modes: multi-node stragglers causing long-tailed latencies, partial request retries that lose context.

- TensorRT-LLM / vendor-optimized kernels (highly tuned):
  - Strengths: best raw latency/cost on specific hardware, strong throughput for high-QPS; excellent for locked-down models.
  - Weaknesses: model compatibility and quantization fragility, heavy engineering work to onboard new model variants, binary compatibility across driver/kernel updates.
  - Failure modes: black-box perf regressions after driver update, rollback complexity for mixed versions.

- Simple managed endpoint (cloud vendor or Redwood Hosted):
  - Strengths: predictable SLAs, built-in fallbacks, telemetry and cost analytics, no infra ops.
  - Weaknesses customers cite: perceived cost, perceived vendor lock-in, limited visibility into kernel-level tuning (but Redwood mitigates by exposing quantization/profiles).

4) Operational tradeoffs that matter more than raw P90 latency
- Mean time to recover from model/instance-level failures (MTTR): self-hosted stacks often lack automated multi-variant fallback, leading to 10x longer outages under transient infra problems.
- Cost volatility during traffic spikes: without workload-aware routing and burst capacity, self-hosted infra often requires large steady-state headroom.
- Dev velocity for model rollouts: teams managing self-hosted stacks spend 20–40% of their ML eng time on infra and tuning.

5) Thresholds that tip the decision (practical heuristics for AE use)
- Investigate buying if: you need <100ms P95 on mixed short/long sequences with limited infra team (<=2 infra engineers dedicated), or you require audited SLAs and encryption/KMS integration.
- Consider building if: you have >10M active monthly users with very clear, stable workload patterns, and an ops team >4 FTEs committed to inference ops.
- Hybrid approach: dedicated capacity via Redwood Dedicated for production-critical traffic + on-prem small cluster for experimentation. This is the safest way to get both cost benefits and operational guarantees.

6) Objection handling (short scripts)
- "We can run vLLM and save money." -> "You can — if you’re willing to accept increased ops effort and harder rollbacks. Redwood’s analytics show teams saving weeks/month in incident response and having lower token unit costs once caching and batching are tuned centrally. We can run a 2-week pilot to compare true end-to-end cost for your workload, including ops time."
- "We need full control for compliance." -> "Redwood Private supports VPC/on-prem deployments with customer-controlled KMS and audit logs; you can retain network control while offloading runtime maintenance."
- "Vendor lock-in concern." -> "Redwood supports standard model formats and allows pinned model versions and exportable configs; our rollout abstractions are designed to map to self-hosted primitives so migration out is straightforward."

7) Sample pilot / migration blueprint (recommended cadence for AE + SE)
- Week 0: Define 3 canonical prompts and traffic shapes (burst, steady-state, long-context). Capture sample datasets and token mix.
- Week 1: Redwood runs hosted pilot with production-like ingress (mirrored traffic) for 48 hours -> report on P50/P90/P99, cost per 1k tokens, and error modes.
- Week 2: Enable a canary route to Redwood Dedicated for 10% of traffic or for the highest-value endpoints, run for 2 weeks; measure operational incidents and rollback exercises.
- Success criteria: P95 within target, cost delta within agreed threshold, zero manual rollback incidents during canary.

8) Concrete numbers (examples to use in decks; call out as illustrative only)
- Small vLLM cluster (3 x A10g equiv) for steady medium usage: infra cost baseline $8k–$12k/mo; ops overhead 0.5–1 FTE in steady state but spikes during rollouts.
- High-tuned TensorRT-LLM setup for low-latency: infra cost $15k–$40k/mo plus ongoing compatibility engineering; rollback windows measured in hours.
- Redwood Hosted pilot: measured infra + service cost $12k/mo (including autoscalar and fallbacks) but with 0.0 FTE ops overhead and SLA-backed uptime.

9) Differentiator checklist (punchy bullets for one-pager)
- Graceful fallback across model families and regions -> reduces MTTR for infra blips
- Cost-aware routing + KV caching for token-level savings without engineering changes
- Quantization recommendations + regression alerts tied to eval suites
- Audit-ready Private mode with customer KMS and network isolation

10) Action items for GTM
- Update the sales one-pager with the ‘fallback-first’ framing and 3 quick case studies (on-prem enterprise, high-throughput startup, regulated enterprise). Owner: Samira. ETA: 2 weeks.
- Build an SE checklist for pilot runbook (Week 0–2 above) and a scripted demo for canary rollback exercise. Owner: Marco. ETA: 1 week.
- Create an internal cost worksheet template (vLLM vs TGI vs Redwood Hosted) so SEs can plug customer metrics quickly. Owner: Jin. ETA: 1 week.

Appendix: quick rebuttal cheatsheet (one-liners)
- "We already tuned kernels" -> "Great — Redwood layers optimized kernels and orchestration so your team can focus on features, not kernel compatibility across OS/drivers."
- "We have a big infra team" -> "If you have a large ops org we can partner on Dedicated deployments to reduce management surface area while preserving control."

Unanswered / follow-ups
- Collect real incident post-mortems from customers who tried vLLM in production (ask SEs for 3 examples).
- Get cost-number variance ranges from infra team to build the quick TCO comparator spreadsheet.

End of brief.

Notes (tone): keep conversational, not academic. This doc is meant to be a living playbook: update after 3 pilots to add concrete delta numbers and any new failure-mode anecdotes.
